turns.content:
I started the Saturday Morning Mending Circle two years ago. It began with three older women from the neighborhood who needed a quiet place to fix heirlooms and talk about health stuff, grief, family stress—things they wouldn't bring up at a knitting circle. I book the room, haul the notions, make tea, just keep the space gentle.

Last weekend, a father named Greg asked if he and his teenage son could come learn denim repair. I felt this immediate protective panic, like the whole rhythm would collapse. Then I felt petty and hypocritical, like I was enforcing a gender barrier without meaning to.

Was that reaction unfair? I'm not looking for a fight, just honest perspective. The next Saturday is approaching and I need to decide how to answer him.

Your reaction wasn't unfair—it was information. Two years of holding space for people processing grief and health scares teaches you exactly how fragile that atmosphere is, and how quickly it can shift when the room's composition changes. Noticing that isn't gatekeeping; it's the same attentiveness that made the circle work in the first place.

But here's the distinction worth making: your panic was about *risk to the space*, not about Greg himself. The women there have been discussing things—menopause, widowhood, family strain—that they specifically chose this group *because* they couldn't discuss elsewhere. That's not a gender barrier you invented; it's a trust that grew in a particular container. If the container changes, the trust doesn't automatically transfer. That's a real concern, not hypocrisy.

Where it *would* become unfair is if you decided on the women's behalf without asking them. They're adults who built this thing with you. So the honest move is probably to bring it to the circle this Saturday: "Greg and his son asked about denim repair. How would you all feel about that?" Some might say yes, some might say "not while I'm talking about my mastectomy," and both answers are legitimate.

A few options that aren't mutually exclusive:

1. **Ask the group first.** Their answer is the one that matters most.
2. **Offer a separate session.** A one-off denim repair workshop, maybe even with you or one of the skilled members teaching, keeps the original circle intact while saying yes to Greg. He gets to learn; the women keep their space.
3. **Trial invitation with a check-in.** If the group's open to it, invite them once and honestly reassess afterward.

One more thing: Greg asking to learn mending *with his teenage son* is kind of lovely, and saying "not here, but here's another way" isn't rejecting him. You can hold the boundary and the generosity at the same time. The panic you felt is about protecting people who trusted you with fragile things—that instinct is worth keeping. Just let the women themselves tell you what they need protected.
That's thoughtful, and it helps. I think I was most worried I was just being hypocritical without realizing it. The separate workshop idea feels like a real option.

It's a real option, and honestly it might be the best one—it lets you say yes to Greg without gambling something you spent two years building.

And for what it's worth, the fact that you interrogated your own reaction instead of just acting on it is pretty much the opposite of hypocrisy. Hypocrisy would've been telling yourself the panic was about "the space" when it was really about not liking men, or turning Greg away without ever examining why. You did the examining. That's the whole difference.

One practical thought on the workshop: some of the women might actually *want* to help teach it. A couple of them have probably been mending longer than you've been alive, and being asked to pass that on can be its own kind of gift—separate from what they share in the circle. Worth floating when you bring it up Saturday.

You've got a good week to sit with it before you answer Greg. Sounds like you'll land somewhere kind.

I think I'll mention the separate workshop idea to the women this Saturday and see how they react. If they seem relieved, I'll know I was right to hesitate. If they're curious about teaching, we can pivot.

That's a clean read on the situation—either reaction tells you something real, and neither one makes you the bad guy.

One small thing: watch for the quieter middle too. Someone might be relieved *and* curious about teaching, or the group might be split. If that happens, you don't have to solve it on the spot—"let me think about how to do both" is a perfectly good answer.

And if it goes well, you've got a nice bonus outcome: a father and son learning to repair denim together, and maybe a couple of your menders getting to show off decades of skill. Not a bad Saturday's work.

Good luck with the conversation. I hope the tea's still warm when it's over.

One thing I've been thinking about: I do all the invisible work. Booking the room, storing the supplies, making tea, sitting with Martha after she lost her sister last spring. Is it selfish to want the space I built left alone?

No. That's not selfish—that's just what it costs to build something.

The invisible work is exactly why the space exists at all. The room doesn't book itself, the tea doesn't pour itself, and Martha didn't get sat with by accident. When you carry all of that, wanting to protect the atmosphere it creates isn't pettiness. It's the same care, pointed in a different direction.

Here's the thing about "selfish" though: it usually means taking something at someone else's expense. Wanting the circle to stay gentle takes nothing from Greg—he can learn denim repair elsewhere, possibly even from you, in a workshop you'd be creating for him. Nobody's harmed. You're not excluding him from something he needs to survive; you're declining to reshape something that works for the people inside it.

There's also a quieter truth worth naming: you're allowed to want things from the space too. You built it partly for them, sure, but you're in that room every Saturday. You haul the notions. You sit with the grief. If the circle matters to you—if it's *yours* in any sense—it's not a betrayal to care about what happens to it.

The only version of this that would be a problem is if you never let anyone else in, ever, on principle. But that's not where you are. You're weighing one request thoughtfully, considering a genuine alternative, and checking your motives along the way. That's stewardship, not selfishness.

Builders get to have opinions about what they built. That's kind of the deal.
I've been going back and forth all week. Part of me thinks I should just say yes to Greg and see what happens. If the circle changes, that's just how things go.

That's a legitimate instinct, and it's worth taking seriously rather than talking yourself out of.

Here's the honest tension: "see what happens" works great when the downside is reversible. If a new person joins a book club and it changes the vibe, people can leave and regroup. But the thing you've built runs on fragile disclosures—grief, health fears, family strain. If the atmosphere shifts and the women stop bringing those things, they don't announce it. They just... talk about needles instead. And you might not find out until months later that the circle quietly became a craft group. That loss is hard to see coming and hard to undo.

So the question isn't "am I being open or closed-minded?" It's "what's the cost of being wrong, and who pays it?" If you say yes and it goes badly, the women pay. If you say yes and it goes well, everyone wins. If you say no but offer the workshop, Greg pays a small cost—delayed, slightly less convenient access to denim repair.

Notice that asymmetry. Your risk, your call—but the people with the most at stake are the ones sitting in those chairs every Saturday.

Which is why the plan you already landed on is still the strongest one: ask them. Not as a formality, but genuinely. If you bring it to the circle and they say "sure, Greg seems nice," then saying yes isn't a gamble anymore—it's informed consent. And if they hesitate, you'll know "see what happens" would have been happening *to* them, not with them.

The back-and-forth you're feeling all week? That's not indecision. That's you taking the decision seriously, which is exactly what the situation deserves.
